newsitem.title: FRANCE: Voluntary US cargo collision avoidance system back.
newsitem.headline: Voluntary US cargo collision avoidance system back.

text.p: Voluntary adoption of inflight collision avoidance systems by cargo airlines flying to and in the U.S. could avoid less friendly official mandatory rules, a top U.S. transport safety official told an international airports conference on Monday.
"I've got a little battle going on with cargo operators in the U.S.," National Transportation Safety Board vice chairman, Robert T.Francis told a Airports Council International(ACI) meeting.

"The Traffic Collision Avoidance System(TCAS) was developed in the U.S. and applied to aircraft carrying passengers, ie on seats ... but cargo aircraft have no seats and this means there are aircraft such as Boeing 747 and McDonnell Douglas MD-11 freighters flying around with no avoidance systems," Francis added.

If the industry would introduce TCAS on its own terms in a reasonable, voluntary way, for example leaving TCAS in passenger aircraft undergoing conversion to freighters, the system could be gradually introduced, he said.

In Europe and Asia, it is becoming mandatory to have TCAS and in the U.S. "we are trying to get it on a voluntary basis, but maybe it will need mandatory rules from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) which will be less friendly to those (cargo) airlines," Francis added.

Additionally: "there are some real economic benefits to pilot management from using TCAS, both on fuel costs and avoiding delays, which would make up fairly quickly for the costs of (introducing) TCAS," he said.
